label: paragraph_title
text: SCHOLARS OR MEN?

label: text
text: If the discussion arising out of the debate at the last meeting of the Education Board has done no evident good, it has, so far, done no harm. At least two of those who have unburdened themselves on the question of ained against untrained teachers, have indicated the desirability of turning out not merely scholars from our schools, but men. The story is being related of the American professor, taken round the German universities remarking: "I have seen the universities where they make scholars; now I am going to look at the universities where they make men." He was asked where and replied: "In England, of course." Highly complimentary and doubtless true. The turning out of men seems to be the dominating desire of the National Union of Teachers. At their annual conference at Oxford last month, the president made it clear that "as in our universities, so in the common schools, our main purpose is the making of men." They did not place so much importance on intellectual training as they did in the moulding of "character and habits, because "the character and habits that run through all our work are of more consequence than mere knowledge." The most important thing in education, the President stated, was the human factor. No amount of organisation no number of inspectors or directors could equal the personality of a good teacher. Such ideas as these tend to a spirit of hope in the future of the race. A policy with these

label: text
text: aims, may lose us' much in scholarship—although it is difficult to realise it or to agree with it; but so it turns out men of merit, the rest may well be added to it. Just as a Court of Law is not necessarily a court of morals, it may be held that a school is not necessarily a place of character building, but a place where things are taught. But he would be a fool who would suggest that education is the one thing only to aim at. We seem to have a superfluity of clever boys, but not an overplus of those whose influence for good is likely to weigh to any great extent. Let education and character building go hand in hand.

label: paragraph_title
text: British Labour and Moscow.

label: text
text: A conference on trade union internationalism, arranged by the General Council of the Trades Union Congress, was held in London in mail week, when a Russian delegation under M. Tömsky was present. It is difficult to understand why British Labour should think it necessary to flirt in this way with Bolshevism. There is practically nothing in common between British trades unionism and the camouflaged serfdom of the Russian variety. British Labour leaders are anxious enough in public to dissociate themselves from Moscow's doings and grow very angry when they are classed with the Bolsheviks. Nevertheless, they seem to have a perpetual desire to make "gestures" and to hold out hands to Moscow. Among the members of the conference in mail week there were trade union leaders, like Mr. Will Thorne, who have never disguised their distrust of the Red International. Possibly one explanation is that since the extreme left of the Labour movement is much under the influence of Moscow, the wiser Labour leaders, to avoid the charge of obscurantism, are willing to let the divergences appear by means of public conferences. British Labour was shipwrecked last autumn on its weakness for Moscow, and it will never regain its prestige so long as its internationalism is suspected in the public mind of leanings to what is neither nationalism nor internationalism, but a naked tyranny.

label: paragraph_title
text: Women Teaching Boys.

label: text
text: Teachers seem to take their duties seriously. At Home recently there has been a conference of teachers, and a conference of schoolmasters. This latter body is greatly perturbed at the number of women who are teaching boys. There are 3,240 women teachers in boys departments, but only two men in girls departments. "If boys are to be trained as men, to act as men and to think as such, they must have many instincts planted in them. This

label: text
text: cannot be done by women teachers." Let those who know, fight it out. The contention seems reasonable. Although in an age of athletics when we have girl and women champion swimmers, tennis, hockey and football players; harriers, and all the rest of the tribe of so-called "unmanly" women, the implied contention that women teachers are not capable of implanting what are known as manly instincts, seems a little unfounded. The profession of teaching—taking a general view—seems peculiarly a feminine one, and the incursion of women is not likely to retard the production an A1 race. On the contrary.

label: doc_title
text: TRAVEL IN JAPAN.

label: text
text: THOS. COOK & SON'S REPORT.

label: text
text: Messrs. Thos. Cook & Son, Ltd., have given us some interesting information regarding travel conditions to and in Japan.

label: text
text: Many people are under the impression that the disorganised condition of Japan, the result of the terrible catastrophe in September, 1923, still prevails. This is entirely erroneous. Travel, both by rail and road, has returned to the normal and the many beautiful places known to the older residents of the Colony are again well worth visiting. It is unnecessary to eulogize Japan to those who have travelled in this picturesque country and space forbids us mentioning even briefly the many wonderful scenes of indescribable beauty which can be visited by those with the most modest incpmes. There is a good and frequent service of steamers from Hongkong to Japan and the journey can be made in the matter of five days or so. From arrival in Kobe any part of the country may be visited in a very short time.

label: text
text: So many residents delay their holiday in Japan with the idea of passing through Kobe and Yokohama en route for Home, with the result they do not see the country at all either because of unexpected circumstances arising preventing them from travelling that way or perhaps anxiety to reach home quickly destroys their good intention. In any case Japan deserves something more than a cursory view from a port or perhaps a train between Kobe and Yokohama.

label: text
text: Although the luxury tax has been imposed on so many foods, etc., in Japan, it is interesting to note that at the general meeting of the members of the Japan Hotel Association held at Secul last September, it was unanimously decided that the hotels should not raise their rates. In addition the Government Railway have not raised their tariff since 1920 and the sundry expenses incidental to travel, such as rotor car charges, ricsha fares, etc., have not been increased.

label: text
text: In conclusion, mention should be made of the favourable rate of exchange between the Hongkong Dollar and the Yen which, at present, would make a holiday in Japan about 80 per cent, cheaper than if the currencies were normal.

label: text
text: Residents who are thinking of taking a holiday are well advised to call on Messrs. Thos. Cook & Son, Ltd., who will give them every assistance in planning the trip, which they are in an exceptional position to do, having representatives in both Kohe and Yokohama.

Shiny, radiant, smiling headpiece,
Crown of awe-inspiring nod;
Fashions change in cloth and leather.

Born to set the nations quaking

label: text
text: Mr. Maugham's new novel is set, suitably enough, in China, a land of pitiless, sunshine. It is the story of a marriage; a tragedy silhouetted against a brilliant background. Mr. Maugham shows himself as clear-sighted as ever, but he allows here a degree of suffrance to fool and sinners (self-convicted as such) which takes the bitterness from the truths he brings to light. Technically, like all Mr. Maugham's work, the book is a joy.
